rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's offer shows his readiness to risk his own life and honor to protect his guests; the people should rebuke themselves for violating their guests' honor.
rows.anchor: ready to put his own life and honour at stake to save the life and honour of another person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's affectionate assurance means Lot should not grieve over people who can no longer mend their ways; God's punishment will decide their fate.
rows.anchor: now there is no chance of these people mending their ways and so the Prophet (sws) should not fret over them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣayhah means a shout and here denotes the punishment that overtook Lot's people at daybreak.
rows.anchor: means “a shout.” Here it refers to God’s punishment that visited the people of Lot (sws) as soon as it was daybreak.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The storm wind's thunder and lightning explain why the author considers the word ṣayhah apt for the punishment.
rows.anchor: The stormy wind was accompanied with the roar and glare of thunder and lightening.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the verse concisely refers to the punishment's nature and introduces Farāhī's detailed account of it.
rows.anchor: This verse rather concisely refers to the nature of punishment that came to them. My mentor, ustāz Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī, has explained

rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī describes a sand-laden wind forming clay stones, pelting Lot's people, then intensifying until their houses were overturned and buried by sand and pebbles.
rows.anchor: My mentor, ustāz Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī, has explained in detail its nature in his exegesis of Sūrah Dhāriyāt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi directs readers to Farāhī's al-Fīl commentary for his research on the word sijjīl.
rows.anchor: is presented by him in his exegesis of Sūrah al-Fīl thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author relays Farāhī's etymology of sijjīl as Persian sang, stone, plus gil, clay; the Qur'an explains it through pebbles of sijjīl and clay stones.
rows.anchor: is Arabicized form of two Persian words sang (stone) and gil (clay).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawassum means observing something closely and drawing a lesson from it as an example.
rows.anchor: means to minutely observe and learn a lesson from something exemplary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression sabīl muqīm means a commonly trodden way.
rows.anchor: means “a commonly trodden way.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are urged to learn from ruined nations, whose remains they pass on trade routes; Sodom and Gomorrah lay on the Hijaz–Syria route.
rows.anchor: They actually observe their remnants on the trade-routes they often pass by. It may be kept in mind that the settlements of Sodom and Gamorrah were situated on the trade routes of Ḥijāz and Syria.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account is a sign for believers: the righteous may be tested, yet ultimately receive God's mercy while their enemies are defeated.
rows.anchor: though the righteous are put through trials but ultimately it is they who become worthy of God’s mercy and their enemies are routed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next section recounts other nations' rejection and destruction, then assures the Prophet to keep calling, remain patient, and expect eventual success with his companions.
rows.anchor: the succeeding verses, the anecdotes of some other nations who denied their respective messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Naḥl presents the messenger's eventual victory and the rejecters' defeat: verse 30 links good conduct to good in this world and better reward hereafter, while verses 41–42 promise authority and reward to oppressed migrants.
rows.anchor: The conflict between truth and falsehood that ensues with the advent of a messenger necessarily culminates in his victory and that of his followers and in the defeat of his rejecters.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥijr closes by assuring the Prophet not to be upset by mockery because God will take the arrogant to task; al-Naḥl opens directly with the announced divine directive.
rows.anchor: The previous sūrah – al- Ḥijr – ended on a note of assurance for the Prophet (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–9 warn Quraysh that punishment approaches, reject reliance on partners, affirm accountability for purposeful creation, and direct people toward God's straight path.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers of the Quraysh are warned that they should know that God’s torment is just about to arrive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should follow God's straight path and avoid deviant paths, although God could have guided everyone had He willed.
rows.anchor: the correct attitude for people is to adopt the straight path delineated by Him and avoid treading on deviant paths.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet warned that people who rejected his message would be punished after their period of respite expired.
rows.anchor: if they do not accept his message, they would be punished by God once their period of respite expires.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The announced punishment is a fact, reflecting God's practice that a messenger's believers are saved and rejecters destroyed after conclusive communication leaves them only faith or wrath.
rows.anchor: The words “the directive of God has been pronounced” do not merely sound a threat; they state a fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is peerless, and the deities the disbelievers rely on cannot save them from His punishment or rival His attributes.
rows.anchor: He is peerless and does not have any partners. There is absolutely no relation of superstitious beliefs with His exalted attributes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from direct to indirect address suits the warning in the first clause and conveys abhorrence and turning away in the second.
rows.anchor: The first part consists of warning and threat; hence direct address is more appropriate for it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 1 addresses the demand for punishment; verse 2 addresses the demand for angels, who descend only on servants God chooses, as verse 33 anticipates.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers had two demands: first, they wanted angels to descend on them too the way they do on the Prophet (sws) as per his claim;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation accompanying God's directive is called rūḥ because spiritual life, like bodily life, depends on this divine revelation.
rows.anchor: just as bodily life can only exist because of the soul, the soul can only exist because of God’s revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus's teaching that life depends on God's word supports the image of revelation as soul; every messenger is told to proclaim God's sole deity and call people to fear and worship Him alone.
rows.anchor: but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.” (Matthew, 4:4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaqq means purpose or objective; the world's wisdom and gradual development show creation is purposeful, which entails a return to God for judgment or else makes the world meaningless.
rows.anchor: means “purpose” and “objective.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about God's superiority reinforces purposeful creation: idolaters reject the hereafter and rely on intercessors, but their associates cannot benefit them or share God's attributes.
rows.anchor: The words “He is superior to things which they associate with Him” emphasize what is stated above in another way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here human being refers to the idolaters and disbelievers under discussion, who are left unnamed to express the author's aversion to them.
rows.anchor: They are not named to express aversion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human, made from an impure drop, becomes God's inveterate enemy and denies resurrection; the source links this hostility to the coming challenge over God's associates.
rows.anchor: such is the audacity of a human being created from an impure drop of water that he has become an inveterate foe of God
